central_question: Why does your phone screen get smudged even when you never touch it?
hook: A spotless phone screen suddenly turns greasy in seconds—no touch, no dirt, just a slick film that looks like a fingerprint. How can a glass surface become oily without anyone ever touching it?
aha_moment: The screen’s protective oleophobic coating wears thin over time, letting airborne skin‑oil droplets and static charge pull oily particles onto the glass, so smudges form even without touch.

story_arc.reveal: A clean phone instantly looks greasy
required_facts: Phone screen appears oily after a quick wipe

story_arc.reveal: Thin fluoropolymer repels oil, keeping screens clear
required_facts: Oleophobic coating is a low‑surface‑energy fluoropolymer

story_arc.reveal: Each swipe, wipe, or heat exposure removes nanometres of polymer
required_facts: 100‑200 k touches thin the coating enough for oil to wet glass

story_arc.reveal: Humans emit 0.5–2 mg h⁻¹ of sebum that condenses into sub‑micron droplets
required_facts: Skin‑oil aerosols settle on surfaces even without touch

story_arc.reveal: Phones acquire static charge in dry air, pulling oily particles
required_facts: Low relative humidity increases surface charge, attracting oil

story_arc.reveal: People think only fingerprints cause smudges, but airborne oil and static do the job
required_facts: Myth: only fingers create fingerprints – reality: airborne skin‑oil can deposit smudges

story_arc.reveal: Coating wear, airborne oil, and static together explain smudges without contact
Cleaning can accelerate coating loss; gentle wipes and protective films help
required_facts: Harsh cleaning accelerates coating loss; protective films may attract static

ending_payoff: Now you’ll know that every time you glance at your phone, unseen skin‑oil particles and a thinning protective film are silently turning your screen greasy—so the next time it looks slick, you’ll see the hidden chemistry at work.
